1.pericope_label: Judah turns aside to Adullam, marries a Canaanite, and has three sons

schools.summary: Gill ties 'at that time' to the selling of Joseph and defends the date by arithmetic: only twenty-three years remain before Jacob goes down into Egypt, but all of it can be accounted for if Er and Onan each married at seventeen, with two or three years allowed for Tamar's waiting on Shelah. On the wife's father he reports that the Targums render the word merchant rather than Canaanite, a rendering meant to take off the disgrace of the match. Calvin supplies the frame for the whole chapter: Moses inserts Judah's genealogy before resuming the story of Joseph because the Redeemer was to spring from that tribe, and what he sets down is not the tribe's nobility but the family's deepest disgrace, which ought to cover the sons of Judah with shame. At first sight Christ's dignity seems tarnished by such dishonour; but here too is that emptying of which Paul speaks, and it adds to his glory, for we wrong him unless we hold him alone sufficient to blot out any ignominy from his progenitors. He derives no glory from his ancestors, his chief triumph being on the cross, and by his infinite purity they were all cleansed, as the sun draws up whatever impurities are in earth and air and so purges the world. On the marriage itself Calvin will allow no softening: Moses charges Judah with perverse lust in taking a wife out of the very nation Abraham's children were commanded to be at perpetual strife with, and God at length cursed the offspring, so that neither the head of the tribe nor Christ should descend from that connection.

Henry reaches Calvin's conclusion from the other end, wondering that of all Jacob's sons our Lord should spring from this one, and finding in it proof that God's choice is of grace and not of merit — so that the Jews who took their name from this Judah had little reason to boast of it. On Judah's conduct he notes that he withdrew for a time from his father's house and grew intimate with an Adullamite, and draws the lesson that when young people who have been well educated change their company they soon change their manners and lose their education, those who forsake the seed of Israel and pick up Canaanites for companions going down the hill apace. He adds that the marriage was made not by Judah's father, who seems not to have been consulted at all, but by this new friend, one wicked league entangling a man in the next.

Clarke will not have the chapter where it stands. The facts recorded here could not have happened at the time of the preceding chapter, which is far too recent for them; and he supposes the chapter originally stood after the thirty-third and got into this place by accident. Wesley speaks with Henry on Judah's conduct, that the withdrawal from his father's house and the new intimacy at Adullam were the beginning of the mischief, and that changed company means changed manners.

Ellicott rejects the early date outright: twenty-two years is scarcely long enough for what this chapter records. He observes that on the usual reckoning Judah would have been barely a year older than Joseph, whereas the truer chronology makes him Joseph's senior by twenty years, so that these events probably began soon after the arrival at the tower of Eder. On the wife's father he notes that our own version renders the word merchant in the Proverbs, but doubts the two senses had become interchangeable so early. He places Adullam in the valley of Elah and explains the going down not by the compass but by the ground, the road being a real descent from the hill country into the lowland. Keil dates the events after the sale of Joseph with Gill, and answers the charge of interpolation before it is made: the narrative shows both the origin of the three leading families of the princely tribe and the danger the sons of Jacob stood in of perishing in the sin of Canaan, had not God's mercy led Joseph into Egypt — which makes it no interpolation but an integral part of the history.

6.pericope_label: Er and Onan die, and Tamar is sent home to wait for Shelah

schools.summary: Gill reads Er's wickedness as meaning exceedingly wicked, some heinous sin left unnamed, and reports the rabbinic guess that it was the same as his brother's, committed lest his wife should lose her beauty — objecting that it would then have been expressed as his brother's was. On Onan he adds a possible covetousness after the estate, and notes what made the refusal worse, that it checked the multiplying of Abraham's seed, the Messiah being to come of Judah. Calvin turns from the crime to the early death: long life is reckoned among God's gifts, so that when the wicked are cut off untimely a punishment is inflicted, as though the Lord pronounced them unworthy to be sustained by the earth; yet long life never proves a man acceptable, God having sometimes lengthened the life of reprobates, and here the vengeance was so remarkable that the earth might appear purged of its filthiness. He grounds the levirate custom in nature rather than statute, each man being born for the preservation of the race, so that when one dies childless there seems a defect in nature and it was an act of humanity to procure some name for the dead — on which reasoning Tamar was held under obligation to the house of Judah, and it was outrageous in Onan to deny a brother what men freely grant to friends in adoption. On Onan's act itself Calvin holds it horrible to pour out seed apart from the union of man and woman, since a man so quenches the hope of his family, and says Onan tore away his brother's seed as by a violent birth and cast it on the ground. He is harshest of all on Judah, who kept bound a woman he meant to defraud and had no cause to refuse her freedom except that he dreaded the charge of inconstancy; his judgment was wrong, since without weighing the true cause of his sons' deaths he shifted the blame to an innocent woman. Let us learn, Calvin says, not to transfer our blame, and to beware lest a foolish shame so prevail that while we keep our reputation among men we are careless of a good conscience before God.

Clarke likewise says we are not told what Er's wickedness was, but holds that the words in the sight of the Lord prove a very great evil, and points out that the Hebrew word for his wickedness is his own name reversed, as if the writer had said the man was altogether abandoned. On Onan he states the common opinion, that the sin was self-pollution, and calls it a mistake: the crime was the refusal to raise up seed to his brother. Wesley keeps the older reading and presses it home, that sins which dishonour the body are displeasing to God and that thousands still destroy their own souls by this very thing. On Judah's holding of Tamar he agrees that if he never meant to give her Shelah it was an inexcusable prevarication, since it was his sons' own wickedness that slew them; yet he notes that Tamar acquiesced and waited the issue.

Ellicott treats the levirate as older than Moses and explains its two objects: to prevent the extinction of a line of descent, a great matter in genealogical days, and to obstruct the gathering of land into few hands. The Mosaic law did not institute but regulate it, confining it to childless deaths and allowing refusal under penalty of disgrace. Behind Onan's refusal he suspects a plainer motive than any scruple, that he wanted the primogeniture for himself. On Judah he finds that he wished to evade the duty for reasons he afterwards owned insufficient, but will not say that he blamed Tamar, since two such losses might frighten any man. Keil supposes the sudden deaths made Judah hesitate, on a superstition also found in the book of Tobit that the woman herself had killed her husbands.

12.pericope_label: Judah goes up to the sheep-shearing, and Tamar sits veiled by the way

schools.summary: Gill remarks on the widow's garments that it was usual in those countries for widows to wear a different apparel in the time of their mourning, what with us is called the widow's weed. He supposes Tamar sat some little distance from the road, so that Judah turned aside to reach her, and that he sent his friend on ahead while he committed the crime. Calvin refuses the charitable construction of Tamar's design altogether: she was avenging an injury, had long meditated the plan and set spies to bring her word of Judah's movements, and desired no connection with him except while she was in a state of celibacy — which he allows as some alleviation, yet holds her hurried by a blind error into a crime no less detestable than adultery, since adultery violates conjugal faith where this subverts the whole dignity of nature. On the veil he takes a line of his own: she dressed after the manner of harlots that Judah might suspect nothing, and God has engraved this sense of shame so deeply on those who live wickedly that they witness against themselves, fleeing the light and struck with horror against their will, so that the veil proves fornication was condemned even by those who practised it. He marks the disgrace on Judah's side as well — he was old, and could not have been captivated by beauty at that distance; God blinded him, since he did not know a voice long familiar to him, and it was folly past explaining to hand a signet to a harlot for the price of a kid.

Henry reports the charitable construction of Tamar's design: that though a Canaanite she had embraced the true religion and believed the promise of a Messiah from Judah's loins, and so desired a child of that family that she might stand fair for the honour of being his mother. If that was indeed her aim it succeeded, since she is one of the four women named in the genealogy of Christ, her sinful practice pardoned and her good intention accepted, which magnifies the grace of God but can by no means justify the like. On the veil he takes it for the custom of harlots in those times to cover their faces, so that though they were not ashamed they might seem to be, the sin of uncleanness not then going so barefaced as it does now.

Wesley repeats Henry's charitable construction of Tamar's motive and his reading of the veil as a harlot's custom. Clarke examines the word rendered harlot and finds it means generally one who prostitutes herself for hire or who lives by the public, so that it might as well be rendered a tavern-keeper; such persons veiled themselves and sat by the highway, and though adultery was a flagrant crime this public prostitution was not.

Keil rules out the border town of Dan and Judah in the plain and fixes on the Timnah in the mountains of Judah, the words about going up settling it; he observes that sheep-shearing was a festival among shepherds kept with much feasting, which is why Judah took his friend along. Ellicott decides the opposite way: the remoter place beyond Bethshemesh, now Tibneh, lay only some seven miles from Adullam, and the flocks there were Judah's own and under Hirah's charge; he adds that Enajim has been identified three miles east of Tibneh on an old road out of Adullam, which he thinks settles it. On Tamar's design he takes a third line from Henry's and Calvin's, that her object was to assert her claim to Er's inheritance; and on the veil he answers that the Jewish commentators all agree this was not a harlot's custom at all, and that since Judah afterwards calls her a consecrated woman he probably took her for a votary of the Phoenician Venus performing the vow required of every such woman once in her life — which is why the hire was a kid, to be sacrificed to the goddess.

20.pericope_label: The kid is sent, the pledge is not recovered, and Judah lets it go

schools.summary: Gill notes that Judah employed his friend the Adullamite and not one of his servants to carry the promised kid, the man having gone with him to Timnath and been privy to all this wickedness and kept the secret — though he would have acted the friendlier part had he dissuaded him. He observes further that 'the men of that place' is rather 'of her place', the woman's place, the messenger supposing she dwelt thereabout, and that he returned only after the strictest inquiry. Calvin puts the first point shortly: Judah sends by the hand of a friend that he may not reveal his ignominy to a stranger. On the abandoned pledge Calvin rejects the reading that would make Judah merely excuse himself as one who had kept his promise; he would rather lose the ring than by spreading the matter give occasion to the speeches of the vulgar, lighter being the loss of money than of character, and he was chiefly afraid of the disgrace arising from his fornication. Men not governed by the Spirit of God, Calvin adds, are always more solicitous about the opinion of the world than about the judgment of God; why, when lust excited him, did it not come into his mind, behold now I shall become vile in the sight of God and of angels?

Clarke stops to complain of the translation: our translators often render different Hebrew words by the same English term, and thus many shades of meaning involving traits of character are lost. Earlier Tamar is called a harlot, the word there being zonah, one who prostitutes herself for money; here it is not zonah but kedeshah, a holy or consecrated person, from a root meaning to make holy or to consecrate to religious purposes, and it must necessarily signify a woman consecrated by prostitution to the worship of some impure goddess. He cites Strabo, who calls the prostitutes of the temple of Venus consecrated female servants, and concludes that impure rites and public prostitution prevailed in the worship of the Canaanites in Judah's day, Astarte and Ashtoreth holding among them the place Venus held among the Greeks and Romans. On Judah's fear of shame he holds that he was not ashamed of the act, for this he does not appear to have thought criminal, but only lest he should fall under the raillery of his companions and neighbours for having been tricked out of his signet, bracelets and staff by a prostitute. Wesley leaves both readings open — either lest his sin should come to be known publicly, or lest he should be laughed at as a fool for trusting a harlot with his signet and bracelets — and then presses the point that Judah expresses no concern about the sin, only about the shame; there are many more solicitous to preserve their reputation with men than to secure the favour of God, with whom lest we be shamed goes farther than lest we be damned.

Keil reads the outcome as a calculation: Judah resolved to leave the pledges with the girl rather than expose himself to ridicule by asking further, having done his part toward his promise — let her take them for herself, that we may not become an object of ridicule — and he remarks what the calculation cost, that the signet and the staff were unquestionably of more value than a young he-goat. Ellicott reads the messenger's question the same way Clarke does, as asking after the kedeshah, and adds a topographical note, that Enajim by the wayside seems to have been the village's full name. On the abandoned pledge he answers Clarke: Judah evidently regards what he had done as shameful, and having his friend's testimony, if needed, to prove he had performed what he promised, he bears the loss rather than let the people know he had been guilty of an act which they too would condemn.

24.pericope_label: Judah sentences Tamar, is confronted with his pledge, and confesses

schools.summary: Calvin agrees that death was meant by the sentence: what the Lord afterwards confirmed by law had already prevailed by custom, that a maid from her espousals should be strictly faithful, so the charge was not fornication but adultery, which Judah prosecuted in his own right as one injured in the person of his son. He presses the further question by what right a private man and a stranger in the land usurped the sword, and answers that Judah did not command her death on his own authority, nor did executioners stand ready at his nod; assemblies were then held in which judgments were passed, and Judah as accuser pronounced upon the punishment as if sentence had already fallen, the offence being verified before she was cited. He thinks Tamar's open reproach proceeded from the desire of revenge, since she does not seek an interview to appease her father-in-law but with a deliberate contempt of death demands him as the companion of her doom. Yet he calls the confession a proof of Judah's honesty, that with no one present to extort it by force or threats he voluntarily stoops and takes the greater share of the blame; and he notes that in confessing the fault Judah says nothing more of punishment, whence we infer that they who are rigid in censuring others are much more pliant in forgiving themselves. That Judah knew her again no more Calvin reads as the evidence of penitence, and as proof that men are by nature imbued with a horror of the crime: whoever attempts to destroy the distinction nature dictates between the base and the honourable engages, like the giants, in open war with God. Gill reads the summons the same way as Calvin's assemblies: she was brought forth not to execution but to the court, to take her trial.

Henry alone reads the sentence as branding rather than death — burnt in the cheek or forehead, stigmatised for a harlot — and adds that if death was intended, then perhaps under pretence of zeal against the sin Judah was contriving to be rid of a daughter-in-law he was loath to marry Shelah to. He turns the story on the reader: it is a common thing for men to be severe against those very sins in others which they allow in themselves, so that in judging others they condemn themselves; and the wickedness most secretly committed and most industriously concealed is sometimes strangely brought to light, to the confusion of those who said no eye sees. Of the sequel he says that Judah never returned to it, and that those do not truly repent of their sins who do not forsake them.

Clarke takes the sentence literally: having ordered Tamar to live a widow in her father's house till Shelah should be marriageable, Judah considered her his son's wife, and burning was anciently the punishment of adultery; as patriarch he held supreme magisterial authority over every branch of his family, so acts here only in his juridical capacity. He cannot get past the irony that where adultery was punished by the most violent death, prostitution for money and for religion was reckoned no crime. On Tamar's motive he differs from Calvin, thinking she was moved by nothing but what was common to all Israelitish women, the desire of children who might be heirs of the promise made to Abraham, and that Judah's delay in giving her Shelah was a breach of truth and an injury done her.

Ellicott adds that later the penalty of burning was narrowed to one who had married both mother and daughter, or to a priest's daughter guilty of unchastity, on which account the Jewish expositors argue that Tamar was of a priestly family, some even deriving her from Melchizedek. Keil, looking forward to the birth, remarks only that the children lay in a position which impedes delivery, and that the circumstance was thought significant enough to found their names upon.

27.pericope_label: The twins are born, and Pharez breaks forth before Zarah

schools.summary: Calvin reads the birth as a judgment softened into a sign. Both Judah and Tamar obtained pardon, the one for his error and the other for her contrivance; yet the Lord, to humble them, caused a prodigy at the delivery. Something similar had happened at the birth of Jacob and Esau, though for another reason, prodigies portending sometimes good and sometimes evil; here the twins bring with them in their very birth the marks of their parents' infamy, a public example that such a crime should be branded with lasting disgrace. He then weighs the midwife's words and finds them ambiguous: some refer the breaking forth to the membrane which encloses the child and is torn at the birth; others, he thinks more correctly, suppose she wondered how Pharez, with the barrier of his brother interposed like an intervening wall, should nevertheless have come out first; to others it looks like an imprecation, as if she had said, let the blame of the rupture be upon thee. Calvin will not decide, holding that Moses points out nothing more than that a prodigy took place. Gill rejects the usual derivation of Zarah's name: it comes not from rising like the sun, as is commonly observed, but from his return, his drawing back his hand and as it were returning to his mother's womb, Hillerus deriving the word by transposition of letters from a root meaning to return; though Jarchi, he reports, took the name from the refulgent appearance of the scarlet thread upon the wrist.

Clarke draws his lesson from the thread: the binding of it about the wrist of the child whose arm appeared first shows how solicitously the privileges of the birthright were preserved, and had the midwife not taken that caution, Pharez would have had the right of primogeniture to the prejudice of his elder brother. And yet Pharez is usually reckoned before Zarah in the genealogical tables, and from him and not from Zarah the line of our Lord proceeds — from which he supposes that the twins were probably conjoined in the privileges of the birthright. He derives Zarah's name from the verb to rise or spring up, applied to the sun rising and diffusing his light. He ends on the impartiality of the sacred writer: the insertion of the chapter proves it, since the facts reflect no credit on the patriarchal history, yet these four were progenitors of the Messiah and their birth had to be recorded. Wesley reads the scene as a figure: the birth was hard to the mother, by which she was corrected for her sin, and the children, like Jacob and Esau, struggled for the birthright; the Jews, as Zarah, bid fair for it and were marked with a scarlet thread as those that came out first, but the Gentiles, like Pharez, a son of violence, got the start of them by that violence which the kingdom of heaven suffers, and attained the righteousness the Jews came short of — yet when the fulness of time is come, all Israel shall be saved.

Keil handles the naming as grammar. The midwife's question he renders, what a breach hast thou made for thy part — upon thee the breach, that is, thou bearest the blame of it; and the word means not a rupture of the mother but a breaking through by pressing forward, whence the child's name Perez, breach or breaker-through. Then the other, with the scarlet thread, came into the world and was named Zerah, because he had sought to appear first, whereas in fact Perez was the first-born, and is even placed before him in the later lists. Ellicott gives the same sense for the name, the rising, especially of the sun, and finds in it an allusion to the red streak placed upon the child's hand.
